findings.title: Choosing identifier a@acmeshop.dev unlocks internal_tools — this survives turning off client traits.
findings.subject: internal_tools

explanation.title: Anyone can switch on internal tools by typing a staff-style email
explanation.what_happened: The production flag service decides who gets internal_tools based on the identifier a visitor supplies. Any identifier matching the staff pattern, such as a@acmeshop.dev, flips internal_tools from off to on. The client key is enough to try it, and no trait or login is involved.
explanation.why_it_matters: The identifier is chosen by the caller and never verified, so turning off client traits does not close this gap.
explanation.business_impact: Outsiders could reach staff-only tools and whatever data or actions they expose, in production.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop granting access from a caller-supplied identifier. Decide staff access on the server after real authentication, or use a verified signed value, then retest.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "internal_tools" to any identity whose identifier matches segment "staff_by_identifier", for example "a@acmeshop.dev". No trait is involved.

findings.title: Secret in a client-visible flag value: payment_config
findings.subject: payment_config

explanation.title: Payment secret exposed in a public feature flag
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the client-side environment key can request the flag list and read the payment_config flag in Production. It contains what looks like a live payment provider API secret, plus a webhook address.
explanation.why_it_matters: Client keys are meant to be visible in apps and browsers, so they are not private. Secrets stored in flag values are effectively public.
explanation.business_impact: Attackers could use the key to act as your payment account, causing fraud, financial loss, customer data exposure, and emergency cleanup costs.
explanation.fix_summary: Revoke and replace the exposed payment secret now, remove it from the flag, and store it in a server-side secrets manager.

evidence.note: secret detected in value at $.api_secret (acme_live_key)

findings.title: Forging role=admin unlocks admin_panel (segment "admins")
findings.subject: admins

explanation.title: Anyone can unlock the admin panel by claiming to be an admin
explanation.what_happened: The system decides who gets the admin panel based on a "role" value the user's own app sends. Our test sent role=admin from outside, and the production flag admin_panel switched from off to on. No password or login was needed.
explanation.why_it_matters: The app trusts a claim the user can make up themselves, so the admin check protects nothing.
explanation.business_impact: Any customer or attacker could reach admin features, risking data exposure, unauthorized changes, and compliance or reputational damage.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop deciding admin access from user-supplied values. Base it on server-verified identity, and enforce admin permissions on the server too.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "admin_panel" to an identity with trait/identifier role="admin" (segment "admins"; forgeable: yes).

findings.title: Users can pick their own group in experiment "Pricing page price test" (pricing_page)
findings.subject: pricing_page

explanation.title: Visitors can choose their own price in the pricing test
explanation.what_happened: Anyone with the public client key can send any identifier they like and see which price variant it receives. By trying identifiers until they land in the low-price group, they can switch from price_high to price_low. Roughly half of the identifiers tried (50.5%) landed in the low-price group.
explanation.why_it_matters: The experiment assumes users are assigned randomly. Letting people pick their group breaks that and corrupts the test results.
explanation.business_impact: Price-savvy visitors can get the cheaper price, reducing revenue, and the test data can no longer be trusted for pricing decisions.
explanation.fix_summary: Assign experiment groups on the server from trusted user IDs, not client-supplied identifiers, and enforce the price on the server when charging.

evidence.note: Variant spread over 1000 identifiers: map[price_high:489 price_low:511]

explanation.title: Secret payment setting is exposed to apps and browsers
explanation.what_happened: The production flag "payment_config" is classified as secret, but its "Server-side only" setting is off. Because of that, client SDKs, which run in users' browsers and apps, receive it.
explanation.why_it_matters: Anyone who uses the app can potentially read the flag's contents. Secret values should only ever be delivered to your own servers.
explanation.business_impact: If the flag holds payment details or keys, outsiders could view or misuse them, risking fraud, compliance trouble, and customer trust. The evidence does not show what the value contains.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for payment_config in the production dashboard. Then check what it contains and rotate any real secrets it held.

evidence.note: Feature "payment_config" is classified SECRET but the dashboard setting "Server-side only" is off, so client SDKs receive it.

findings.title: Traits of ce***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: ce***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: Customer traits readable with public client key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key can request a customer's stored traits by email address. The test showed 3 traits returned for one production identity; values were masked in the evidence.
explanation.why_it_matters: The public key is embedded in apps, so it is not secret. The "Hide sensitive data" setting is off, so personal data is served to outsiders.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal data could be harvested, risking privacy-law penalties, loss of customer trust, and breach notification costs.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Hide sensitive data" for the production environment, and review which traits are stored on identities.

evidence.note: Identity stores 3 trait(s); "Hide sensitive data" is off, so GET identities/?identifier= returns them. Trait values are not read by Gatecrasher.

findings.title: Traits of qa***@acmeshop.dev are readable by anyone with the public client key
findings.subject: qa***@acmeshop.dev

explanation.title: User profile data readable with a public key
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the public client key, which ships inside the app, can look up a user's stored profile traits by their identifier. We confirmed this in production for one test account; one trait was returned.
explanation.why_it_matters: The public key is meant to be visible, so it should never unlock personal data. Anyone could look up users.
explanation.business_impact: Customer personal information could be harvested, creating privacy-law exposure, notification duties, and loss of customer trust.
explanation.fix_summary: Stop returning identity traits to public client keys, or require server-side authentication. Then review which traits are stored.

explanation.title: Anyone can unlock the paid export feature by claiming to be on the gold plan
explanation.what_happened: Using only the public client key, an outsider sent a request stating their plan was "gold". The system accepted this and switched the premium_export feature from off to on. No login or payment check was involved.
explanation.why_it_matters: The plan level is taken from information the user supplies, so it can't be trusted. Anyone can claim any plan.
explanation.business_impact: Free or lower-tier users can use a paid feature without paying, which means lost upgrade revenue and weaker value for paying customers.
explanation.fix_summary: Decide access to premium_export on the server using verified billing data, not user-supplied traits. Remove or restrict the gold_plan segment's reliance on client-provided values.

evidence.note: Flagsmith's engine serves on instead of off for flag "premium_export" to an identity with trait/identifier plan="gold" (segment "gold_plan"; forgeable: yes).

findings.title: Internal URL leaked to every browser: internal_api_url
findings.subject: internal_api_url

explanation.title: Internal admin address exposed in public feature flags
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the client key shipped to browsers can request the flag list and read a flag named internal_api_url. Its value points to a private network address for an admin endpoint.
explanation.why_it_matters: It reveals where internal systems live and that an admin interface exists. That gives an attacker a map for further probing. The evidence does not show the address is reachable from outside.
explanation.business_impact: Easier targeting of internal infrastructure, and a possible step toward a larger breach if other weaknesses exist. Production is affected.
explanation.fix_summary: Remove internal_api_url from flags served to client keys and keep it in server-side configuration. Consider rotating or reviewing anything that relied on that address staying hidden.

findings.title: Re-rolling the identifier unlocks early_access_ai (≈9% rollout, ~11 tries)
findings.subject: early_access_ai

explanation.title: Anyone can retry identifiers until they unlock the early-access AI feature
explanation.what_happened: The early_access_ai flag is meant for a small test group (about 9% of users). Anyone with the public client key can send made-up user identifiers and see which ones get the feature switched on. After roughly 11 tries, one succeeds.
explanation.why_it_matters: Access is decided by a user ID the caller chooses, so the test-group limit is not enforced against outsiders.
explanation.business_impact: Unreleased AI functionality can be seen or used by people who were never invited, risking leaks, unsupported usage, and a spoiled staged rollout.
explanation.fix_summary: Don't rely on client-chosen identifiers for gated access. Check eligibility on the server using trusted account data, and keep unreleased features off the client-facing environment.

findings.title: Production: "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON
findings.subject: allow_client_traits

explanation.title: Anyone can forge user traits in Production
explanation.what_happened: The Production environment lets client apps set their own user traits. Anyone with the public client key, which is visible in the app, can claim any trait they like.
explanation.why_it_matters: Segments that decide who gets access by trait can be tricked. An outsider could label themselves as an admin or paying customer and be placed in that segment.
explanation.business_impact: People could unlock gated or paid features, beta programs, or internal tools without authorization, causing lost revenue and possible exposure of restricted functionality.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn off "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" in Production, and any other environment using trait-based segments for access control. Set traits from your trusted server instead.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Allow client SDKs to set user traits" is ON (allow_client_traits). Anyone holding the public client key can set their own traits, so any segment keyed on a trait can be forged. Turn this setting off for every environment that uses segments for access control.

explanation.title: Production feature flag data is not hidden
explanation.what_happened: The "Hide sensitive data" setting is turned off in the Production environment. This means sensitive information tied to your feature flags is not masked in that environment.
explanation.why_it_matters: Without masking, flag-related data that should stay private may be visible to anyone who can reach it. The evidence confirms the setting is off, but does not show that anyone has actually viewed or taken data.
explanation.business_impact: Customer or internal details could be exposed, raising privacy, compliance, and trust concerns if that data is seen by people who should not have it.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Hide sensitive data" in the Production environment's dashboard settings, then confirm it stays enabled.

evidence.note: Environment "Production": dashboard setting "Hide sensitive data" is OFF (hide_sensitive_data). Sensitive data is not hidden in this environment. Turn this setting on.

findings.title: Unreleased product leaked through flag: project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15
findings.subject: project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15

explanation.title: Secret product launch name exposed in public flag list
explanation.what_happened: Anyone holding the client key used by your app can request the production flag list and see a flag named 'project_nightjar_launch_2026_12_15'. The name reveals an internal codename and a planned launch date of December 15, 2026. The flag's value was empty.
explanation.why_it_matters: Flag names are sent to every client, so unreleased plans are visible to anyone who looks. Only the name leaked, not product details.
explanation.business_impact: Competitors, press, or investors could learn about the launch and its timing before you announce it, weakening your marketing plans and competitive position.
explanation.fix_summary: Rename the flag to a neutral name with no codename or date, and keep launch-related flags out of client-visible environments until release.

evidence.note: unreleased product detected in flag name (codename_launch)

explanation.title: Internal API address is exposed to client apps
explanation.what_happened: The flag "internal_api_url" in Production is not set to "Server-side only", so client SDKs receive it. Anyone using the public app or SDK key could potentially read this value.
explanation.why_it_matters: The flag holds an internal URL that should stay private. Exposing it shows outsiders how your internal systems are named and laid out.
explanation.business_impact: Attackers could use the address to probe internal services, making targeted attacks easier. The evidence shows exposure, not an actual breach.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for this flag in the Production dashboard so client SDKs no longer receive it. Then check other internal-URL flags.

explanation.title: Secret launch flag is visible to client apps

explanation.why_it_matters: The flag name reveals an internal project name and a planned launch date. The evidence shows exposure of the name, not other values.
explanation.business_impact: Competitors or press could learn about the unannounced product and its timing before you announce it.
explanation.fix_summary: Turn on "Server-side only" for this flag in Production. Consider renaming it to something non-descriptive.
